description_en: This 33-bayedphalcādefines the southern edge of the Royal Palace Complex. Dating back to the 18th century the once-openphalcāused to provide resting space for pilgrims. Thephalcā'sextension to the west consists of two rooms, one of them housing a Bhīmasena Shrine. The Bhīmasena statue is believed to have been brought from Dolakha. This shrine is managed by the Haḥkhā Ṭola Sundhāra Samiti and is accessible to the public on special occasions only. A triangular-shaped hole provides an opening between the inside shrine and a shrine on the south side of the building (LAL4126-001). The shrine on the outside is also worshipped as Bhīmasena. A brasstoraṇaframes the hole, the painted eyes and the mace.Kota Pāṭī was restored by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust from 2009 to 2012. The roof was completely rebuilt with new timber, athough most of the historic columns, capitals and small carved windows in the half-story were reused. A new vestibule and gates located in the fourth, fifth, and sixth bays were created in order to provide direct access to the Bhandarkhal Park. The two rooms and four bays at the western end of thephalcāare reserved for religious purposes. After the earthquake, the remaining bays were converted into small shops, cafes, and an ATM lounge.
description_ne: लामो र ३३ वटा कवल भएको यो फल्चा पाटन दरवारको दक्षिणपट्टि रहेको छ । एउटा कवलको लम्बाइ लगभग ३०७ सेमी छ । धेरै जसो काष्ठस्तम्भहरू लगभग सन् १७०० तिरका हुन् । सन् २००८ मा यस फल्चालाई भत्काएर कठमाडौँ भ्याली प्रिजर्भेशन ट्रष्टद्वारा पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको थियो ।
monument_assessment: Heavily damaged (collapsed, demolished, major cracks and structural damages), Rebuilt, Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)
references: Sources and references Sources Final report: RESTORATION OF PATAN ROYAL PALACE COMPLEX, MUL CHOWK, KOT PATI, STONE GATES, KATHMANDU VALLEY PRESERVATION TRUST, JANUARY 2013, AFCP 2009 LARGE GRANT, AWARD # S-NP-400-09-CA-029

historical_events.event_description: Thepāṭīwas partly dismantled in 2008 and subsequently rebuilt by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust. The restoration was financed through a large grant from the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (2009).The restoration report prepared by KVPT reads as follows:"Prior to restoration, Kot Pati rest house was a series of makeshift rooms separated by partition walls. After the successful completion of the restoration program, the rest house now appears in its original configuration as continuous long arcade as documented in historic photographs. As with most of the other buildings in the complex, the Pati’s historical tiled roof had been replaced with machine-made flat pan tiles laid onto the timber battens, causing significant water leakage right through the building. This meant that large sections of the structure had to be dismantled and reconstructed using new timber elements. Out of the 34 carved columns and capitals 31 could be restored and were professionally cleaned and reinstalled in their original positions. All historic pillars required new sections of timber to be grafted to their base sections. Two original windows in the western section of the Pati were restored whereas all other small openings above the arcade had to be made new. The new roof structure and cover were designed in the traditional manner. The redundant horizontal ceiling planks were removed to allow for a more spacious and luminous interior. 1 inch hardwood planking and 3/4 inch marine-grade plywood united the roof timber members to create a strong diaphragm and uniform surface for a water proof membrane. Traditional terracotta roof tiles were then placed on a mud-bed on top of the membrane. The fl ooring was covered with traditional terracotta tiles, fa.ades were rebuilt usingma-apabricks, and the buttresses supporting the brick wall were consolidated.""The restoration of Kot Pati progressed quickly. Partition walls were dismantled so that the space retained its original character as a long arcade. Tiling and soling of the floors was completed, and the back wall’s supporting buttresses were rebuilt. Finally, the entire roof structure and cover was replaced.Detailed Activities:- The existing Kot Pati needed to be almost completely dismantled as it was in a highly dilapidated condition. All redundant partition walls and horizontal ceiling planks were removed.- The missing or damaged stone pavement, plinth edges, and mouldings were recreated following existing historic examples.- The historic plinth was completely re-built along the face of the Pati using edge stones andteliatile.- The cement pavement was removed and the floor of the Pati was repaved with traditional floor tiles (cikã apā)in lime and brick dust (surki)mortar.- The existing roof was removed and a new roof structure was constructed in its place with new closely-space timber joists in a traditional configuration- Hardwood planks and marine-grade plywood unite the roof timber members, creating a strong diaphragm and uniform surface for a waterproof membrane.- Traditional terracotta roof tiles were laid on a mud-bed on top of the membrane.- New windows, designed to mirror the old ones, were installed on the principal facade.
